sec: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits

items.q: Match the following magnesium-lowering drugs — 1) PPI 2) Cisplatin 3) Thiazide … A) Transport-pump inhibition B) Impaired intestinal absorption C) Tubular injury
items.exp: The page separates intestinal malabsorption from tubular injury and defective transport-pump mechanisms. (Book p893)

items.q: The source orders tubular-injury drug associations as cisplatin > ___ > ___.
items.exp: Cisplatin, aminoglycosides and calcineurin inhibitors form the printed tubular-injury ranking. (Book p893)

items.q: For the transport-pump subgroup, assess: I PPIs are placed with renal transport-pump inhibitors. II The source ranks thiazides above loop diuretics.
items.exp: Thiazides > loops appears under transport pumps; PPIs are separately listed under impaired GI absorption. (Book p893)

items.q: A patient with advanced renal failure repeatedly uses magnesium-containing laxatives and becomes lethargic with reduced reflexes. What combination explains the electrolyte risk?
opts: Loss of PTH plus reduced intestinal uptake
items.exp: Magnesium laxatives/purgatives/enemas increase intake; renal failure reduces clearance and predisposes to hypermagnesemia. (Book p893)

items.q: Which is the odd one out among extracellular magnesium-shift causes listed?
items.exp: Cell lysis releases magnesium; refeeding instead favors intracellular shifts and depletion. (Book p893)

items.q: Match the following hypermagnesemia associations — 1) FHH 2) Addison disease 3) Acromegaly … A) Increased mineral absorption B) CaSR loss with reduced Ca/Mg excretion C) Volume loss with mineral conservation
items.exp: The page distinguishes CaSR-mediated renal conservation, volume-loss-related conservation and increased absorption. (Book p893)

items.q: During magnesium therapy for pre-eclampsia, deep tendon reflexes become sluggish. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
opts: Consider magnesium accumulation and reassess therapy
Assume the drug cannot raise serum magnesium
Diagnose hypomagnesemia from the reflex finding alone
Escalate magnesium solely because reflexes are slower
items.exp: Therapeutic magnesium can cause hypermagnesemia; reduced reflexes are a toxicity warning, not an indication for blind escalation. (Book p893)

items.q: Match the following source magnesium bands — 1) 4–6 mEq/L 2) 6–10 mEq/L 3) >10 mEq/L … A) Flaccid paralysis/respiratory failure B) Hypotension/bradycardia/depressed reflexes C) Flushing/headache/sluggish reflexes
items.exp: The table describes progressive toxicity in these ranges, with PTH resistance and hypocalcemia in the 6–10 band. These are approximate teaching bands, not individualized safety limits. (Book p893)

items.q: The source places arrest at >2 mEq/L but flushing/sluggish reflexes at 4–6 mEq/L. What is the most defensible interpretation?
opts: The arrest entry is inconsistent with the severity scale
The rows use mg/dL despite the mEq/L column heading
The first row describes ionized and the rest total magnesium
The first row is a validated threshold after renal adjustment
items.exp: The >2 entry is internally inconsistent with the rest of the table and the stated normal range. It is flagged rather than silently repaired to an unverified number. (Book p893)

items.q: A patient with marked magnesium excess has hypotension, bradycardia and hypocalcemia. What endocrine mechanism is listed for the calcium change?
items.exp: The 6–10 mEq/L row links hypermagnesemia with PTH resistance and hypocalcemia. (Book p893)

items.q: Evaluate: I This source specifies one diagnostic ECG signature for magnesium excess. II An ECG without that signature excludes toxicity.
items.exp: The page calls the arrhythmic findings nonspecific; absence of a signature tracing does not rule out toxicity. (Book p893)

items.q: Match the following interventions — 1) Severe magnesium excess with CKD 2) Immediate antagonism of magnesium toxicity 3) Search for a cause of refractory low K/Ca … A) IV calcium gluconate B) Dialysis C) Measure magnesium
items.exp: Dialysis removes magnesium when clearance is impaired, calcium antagonizes acute effects, and magnesium assessment is essential in refractory electrolyte deficits. (Book p893)

items.q: Potassium remains low despite replacement in a magnesium-depleted patient. Which channel mechanism explains this?
opts: Loss of magnesium inhibition of ROMK promotes K loss
Complete ROMK closure prevents potassium secretion
Activation of NaPi-IIc increases potassium uptake
Blockade of all renal potassium channels
items.exp: The source describes a patulous ROMK channel causing renal potassium loss with severe magnesium depletion. (Book p893)

items.q: Profound magnesium deficiency lowers calcium by impaired ___ and by ___.
items.exp: The effect tree shows both reduced PTH secretion and end-organ resistance leading to hypocalcemia. (Book p893)
